prerequisites.meaning: An integer identifying a text unit in one particular tokenizer's vocabulary.
prerequisites.check: Must two different tokenizers assign the same IDs to 'Dublin'?
prerequisites.answer: No. Each tokenizer has its own vocabulary and its own IDs.

prerequisites.meaning: Nonnegative probabilities for possible outcomes, adding to one.
prerequisites.answer: Yes. All values are non-negative and 0.6 + 0.3 + 0.1 = 1.

prerequisites.meaning: A model predicting the next token from the tokens already present.
prerequisites.check: What input is available before the next answer token is generated?
prerequisites.answer: Only the prompt and any tokens already generated, never later tokens.

diagrams.title: A decoder chat request
diagrams.subtitle: Local chat; fixed weights
trace: The question 'What is the capital of Ireland?' is placed in a user message.
The chat template adds the role and assistant-start formatting expected by the selected checkpoint.
Generation repeatedly predicts another token until stopping or reaching its budget.
The code slices off the input so the returned answer contains new tokens only.
The same helper returns a token count and elapsed seconds for comparison.
diagrams.explanation: A chat interface hides several transformations. First, the user's question becomes a message with a role. A chat template adds the model-specific formatting that distinguishes user text from the assistant reply. The tokenizer converts that formatted input into IDs. The decoder then predicts successive tokens; its generation settings determine how each prediction is chosen. The returned tensor includes both the input and generated continuation, so the helper slices away the input before decoding the answer. No training happens during this call: the model's learned weights stay fixed. The lab compares this decoder workflow with BERT's masked-token prediction and Flan-T5's separate input encoder and output decoder. Those families perform different operations even when their demonstrations use similar questions. The token count and elapsed time describe this measured call, rather than guaranteeing answer quality.
diagrams.check_answer: Because decoder generation returns input IDs followed by the continuation; the helper returns only the new answer.
diagrams.notes:
In short: A local chat call formats a message, generates new IDs and removes the prefix before returning the answer.

Explain: The message contains a role and content. A template adds conversation markers. Tokenisation produces integer IDs. Generation repeatedly appends IDs with fixed weights. Slicing removes the original input before decoding the new answer.

Example: For an illustrative input [1,5] and returned sequence [1,8], slice at position five to keep three generated IDs. The helper counts those three and records its call time. Real requests use the checkpoint's actual template; invented shapes do not predict its wording, speed or quality. Hosted APIs normally return answer text through a different interface.

Ask: Why does the local helper slice at the original input length?

Answer: Decoder generation includes the input prefix. Removing it avoids counting or displaying that prefix as newly generated answer tokens.

Watch out: A correct slice verifies the output boundary, not whether the generated answer is true.

diagrams.title: Choose one next token
diagrams.subtitle: Choose; reuse fixed weights
trace: The lab's five scores [2, 1, 0.5, 0.1, −1] give probabilities about [0.56, 0.21, 0.12, 0.08, 0.03].
Top-k with k=2 retains the two highest-scoring candidates in this example.
Top-p with p=0.8 instead retains three: their cumulative probability first exceeds 0.8.
Removed candidates get zero probability; retained probabilities are renormalised.
Sampling selects one ID, which is appended before the next model call.
diagrams.explanation: The neural model provides logits, unnormalised scores for all vocabulary tokens. Decoding is the policy used to turn those scores into a continuation. Greedy decoding chooses the highest-scoring token; the sample helper instead draws a token from probabilities. Temperature rescales logits: a lower positive value concentrates probability on stronger candidates, while a higher value spreads it. Top-k filtering uses a score threshold based on the kth candidate; ties at that threshold can retain additional tokens. Top-p filtering keeps enough leading candidates to reach a chosen cumulative probability, so its retained count depends on model confidence. The chosen token changes the next prefix and therefore the next prediction. A more diverse output is not necessarily more accurate. The manual loop runs its specified number of steps; it does not contain an explicit end-of-sequence stopping test.
diagrams.check_answer: Yes. The distribution changes with the prefix; a confident distribution needs fewer candidates to reach p.
diagrams.notes:
In short: The decoding loop changes the prefix after one token choice while reusing the same trained model weights.

Explain: The decoder returns vocabulary logits. Temperature rescales them using a positive divisor. Filtering excludes some candidates. Sampling draws one ID from retained probabilities. Appending that ID changes the next input sequence.

Example: The worked scores [2,1,0.5,0.1,−1] produce a distribution whose first three candidates exceed cumulative mass 0.8. The retained candidates are renormalised before a draw. At the next position, model scores can differ because the prefix changed. The manual lab loop runs a fixed short number of steps and does not implement an explicit end-token stop.

Ask: Why can the top-p candidate count change on successive calls?

Answer: The new prefix changes the distribution. A concentrated distribution reaches the threshold with fewer entries than an uncertain one.

Watch out: Temperature and top-p change selection; they neither update the model nor guarantee factual accuracy.

diagrams.title: Core generation and checking
diagrams.subtitle: Fixed weights
trace: Tokenise the fixed story prefix with the core SmolLM2 tokenizer, producing IDs [1,L].
The decoder's final vocabulary row supplies scores [V]; temperature and filters define the selection policy.
Append one selected ID and repeat for the recorded short budget, using unchanged model weights.
Decode the reply and verify its fit; distinct-2 measures repetition rather than factual accuracy.
Token counts, perplexity and final-answer scoring are separate experiments; family/reasoning downloads are optional stretches.
diagrams.explanation: This coherent diagram traces generation with the core checkpoint. Text becomes IDs, the fixed decoder predicts vocabulary scores, and a selection rule chooses another ID. Appending changes the prefix for the next call. Decoding yields a reply for task-specific checking. Other lab activities measure tokenizer pieces, known-text predictability or synthetic answer-scoring rules separately. Their outputs are not inputs to this generation path.
diagrams.check_answer: No. The prefix changes and the fixed model repeats inference; an optimiser update belongs to training.
diagrams.notes:
In short: The core generation path tokenises a fixed prompt, appends selected IDs and verifies the resulting reply.

Explain: Text becomes IDs shaped [1,L]. The fixed decoder predicts vocabulary scores [V]. Greedy selection or sampling chooses another ID. Appending extends the prefix for repetition. Decoding makes text available for a task check.

Example: A 16-step manual continuation uses the same small checkpoint throughout. Record its prefix, temperature and filtering settings before comparing outputs. The diagram traces this coherent generation path only. Token-count tables, perplexity and synthetic final-answer checks are separate experiments, while optional BERT/T5/Qwen reasoning runs create additional workloads with their own evidence.

Ask: Does the repetition arrow imply a model-weight update?

Answer: It changes the token prefix and repeats inference with fixed weights; an optimiser step would belong to training.

Watch out: Do not connect unrelated measurements as if one experiment's output supplied another's input.

diagrams.title: How pre-training learns a language model
diagrams.insert_before_title: The LLM pipeline, in more detail
diagrams.subtitle: Developer training; lab scores
diagrams.explanation: Pre-training learns general language patterns from text. The text supplies both input tokens and known next-token targets. A decoder with a causal mask predicts scores without reading future answers. Cross-entropy measures prediction error, and the optimiser adjusts the learned weights. Developers repeat this across many batches and check held-out text. Post-training then uses instruction examples and feedback to improve assistant behaviour. This is a conceptual process diagram, not a claim that the week 6 lab pre-trains an LLM. The lab loads published weights and compares inference behaviour. The target branch goes directly to the loss. The dashed loop belongs to the weight-update step; post-training happens after pre-training.
trace: For a token sequence [A, B, C, D], inputs [A, B, C] pair with targets [B, C, D].
The first position predicts B using A. The second predicts C using A and B.
The training update changes weights. A later chat request uses those learned weights.
Two assistants can differ because of pre-training, post-training or the application around the model.
diagrams.check_answer: No. It loads pretrained weights and runs inference. The diagram describes how developers trained those weights earlier.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Developer pre-training compares causal predictions with known next-token targets and uses gradients to update weights.

Explain: A shifted target is the next token for each input position. The causal mask blocks later answers. Cross-entropy measures error against known targets. An optimiser uses gradients to update weights. Post-training follows with instructions or feedback.

Example: From tokens [A,B,C,D], inputs [A,B,C] pair with targets [B,C,D]. Logits can have shape [B,L,V] and targets [B,L]. The target branch enters the loss directly; it is not leaked into earlier causal inputs. This explains the developer's training process. The current lab only scores published weights and contains no such optimiser update.

Ask: Does passing labels to the lab's no-gradient perplexity call update model weights?

Answer: No. It returns the prediction loss; learning additionally requires gradient computation and an optimiser step.

Watch out: Keep a metric for checking frozen weights separate from a training loss used for an update.

diagrams.title: Read a local or hosted chat call end to end
diagrams.insert_before_title: Querying a hosted model through an API
diagrams.subtitle: Alternative routes
diagrams.explanation: A local request applies the chat template and creates input IDs before generation. A hosted API accepts role/content messages and lets its provider format and run the model. These are alternative routes; the client does not normally send its locally tokenised IDs to a chat API. Local decoder outputs include the input prefix, which must be sliced away. Hosted chat responses already separate the answer message. Record model, settings, date, usage and time, then check correctness. Keep keys in secrets; availability and usage fields depend on the provider.
trace: Send a user message asking for one sentence explaining tokens.
Set max_new_tokens to a small answer budget for the local call.
Compare the returned answer with the request. The original question should not appear as generated output.
Log local timing or hosted usage and keep the same prompt when comparing models.
diagrams.check_answer: No. Local and hosted models can format and tokenise differently; this shared wrapper does not expose hosted usage.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Local and hosted calls are alternative inference routes with different response formats and available usage evidence.

Explain: Local inference templates and tokenises messages. A hosted API receives structured text requests. The provider formats its supported model input. Local decoder output contains prefix and continuation. Hosted responses normally expose a separate answer message.

Example: The local chat helper returns answer text, generated-ID count and elapsed call time. The shared hosted wrapper returns text or None, so provider usage remains missing in the log. The same fictional question keeps task wording comparable, but tokenizers, settings and timing boundaries can still differ. Neither route updates weights during this demonstration.

Ask: Can a locally counted prompt estimate be presented as the provider's actual usage?

Answer: No. Different templates and tokenizers can change counts; report usage only when the chosen interface supplies it.

Watch out: Do not add another key reader or SDK; the shared provider switch and local fallback handle access.

glossary.meaning: A network that converts input data into numerical representations or distribution parameters.
A network that turns a representation or previous outputs into predictions for the output.
Model-specific formatting used to represent roles and messages as a token sequence.
A positive divisor on model scores that changes how concentrated sampling probabilities are.
The leading token candidates retained by a top-p cumulative-probability threshold.
The elapsed time from a request to its result; first-token latency measures the initial wait.
Rules marking which token pairs an attention operation may use; Boolean conventions vary by API.
The known answer used to measure a model's prediction error.

pitfalls: A fluent answer can still be wrong; output diversity is a different measure from correctness.
Few examples inside a prompt change context, rather than updating the model's weights.
Visible thinking text and a longer token budget do not guarantee a correct final answer.

recap.title: What we learned: language models
recap.question: Longer thinking proves correctness?
recap.notes:
In short: Connect model development, request formatting, token selection and task verification without confusing their measurements.

Explain: Training learns parameters from examples. Inference uses fixed parameters. A tokenizer defines prediction units. Decoding selects output candidates. Evaluation checks whether outputs satisfy the actual task and constraints.

Example: Return to the five illustrative candidate probabilities. Top-p 0.8 retains three candidates, but none of that arithmetic verifies a generated definition. The CPU notebook then supplies actual outputs and measured predictability for its named checkpoint. Stored diagrams and tables expose other architectures and configurations; keep their provenance distinct from the new run.

Ask: Does a longer thinking trace prove that the final answer is better?

Answer: No. Compare completed final correctness, token use and actual elapsed time across representative repeated examples.

Watch out: Do not combine stored and fresh model results into one table without identifying their checkpoints, settings and dates.

vocabulary_notes:
In short: Token IDs, probability distributions and causal prediction make this week's local inference experiments readable.

Explain: An ID is an integer for one vocabulary entry. A tokenizer defines the vocabulary and segmentation. A probability distribution has nonnegative entries adding to one. Causal prediction uses only preceding supplied tokens. These ideas determine the shapes in the lab.

Example: A sequence [1,3] has one batch row and three token IDs. A probability vector [0.6,0.3,0.1] has three possible candidates and sums to one. The numbers illustrate shapes and probability rules; the IDs need not correspond to these words in a real tokenizer. A separate vocabulary length V determines the model's score dimension.

Ask: Can token ID 3 be interpreted as the same word in every tokenizer?

Answer: No. Its meaning depends on the chosen vocabulary. Decode IDs with their own tokenizer and inspect actual pieces.

Watch out: Sequence length counts positions; vocabulary size counts possible token entries. They are different dimensions.
